```{r}
#| label: sample
format_tweet <- function(text, quoted) {
  if_else(
    is.na(quoted),
    paste0("Tweet: ", text),
    paste0("Tweet: ", text, "\n\nQuoted tweet: ", quoted)
  )
}

# Random tweets: one set to develop the prompt, one held out to compare configurations.
# The sampled IDs are stored in the cache, so the sample never changes once drawn.
sample_ids <- cached_sample(paste0("dev-test-", n_per_set), \() {
  set.seed(2026)
  slice_sample(tweets_clean, n = 2 * n_per_set)$id_str
})

sampled <- tweets_clean |>
  filter(id_str %in% sample_ids) |>
  arrange(match(id_str, sample_ids)) |>
  mutate(
    set = rep(c("dev", "test"), each = n_per_set),
    input = format_tweet(full_text, quoted_status.full_text)
  )

dev <- filter(sampled, set == "dev")
test <- filter(sampled, set == "test")

# Tweets rendered as HTML cards. Tweet text from the API is already HTML-escaped.
# `probs`: id, label, p; shown as bars to the right of each card.
tweet_html <- function(df, numbered = FALSE, show_labels = FALSE) {
  labels_shown <- if (show_labels) df$labels else rep(NA, nrow(df))
  pmap_chr(
    list(df$user.name, df$user.screen_name, df$legislator_state, df$created_at,
         df$full_text, df$quoted_status.full_text, seq_len(nrow(df)), labels_shown),
    \(name, handle, state, date, text, quoted, i, labs) {
      paste0(
        '<div class="tweet">',
        if (numbered) paste0('<span class="tweet-number">#', i, "</span>") else "",
        '<div class="tweet-header"><strong>', name, "</strong> @", handle,
        " · ", state, " · ", format(date, "%b %d, %Y"), "</div>",
        text,
        if (!is.na(quoted)) paste0('<div class="quoted">', quoted, "</div>") else "",
        if (!is.na(labs)) paste0('<div class="tweet-labels">5 runs: ', labs, "</div>") else "",
        "</div>"
      )
    }
  )
}

tweet_cards <- function(df, numbered = FALSE, show_labels = FALSE, probs = NULL) {
  cards <- tweet_html(df, numbered, show_labels)
  if (!is.null(probs)) {
    cards <- map2_chr(cards, df$id_str, \(card, id) {
      paste0('<div class="tweet-row">', card, prob_bars(filter(probs, .data$id == .env$id)), "</div>")
    })
  }
  cat(cards, sep = "\n")
}

# The model's probability of each label on one call, as HTML bars
prob_bars <- function(p) {
  p <- arrange(p, match(label, labels))
  rows <- paste0(
    '<div class="prob-row', if_else(p$p == max(p$p), " top", ""), '">',
    '<span class="prob-label">', p$label, "</span>",
    '<span><div class="prob-bar" style="width:', round(100 * p$p), '%"></div></span>',
    '<span class="prob-value">', scales::percent(p$p, accuracy = 1), "</span></div>"
  )
  paste0('<div class="probs"><div class="probs-title">Probability (one call)</div>',
         paste(rows, collapse = ""), "</div>")
}

# Tweets (with `id`) as rows, labels as (slanted) columns, one box per tweet and label.
# Without `counts` the boxes are empty, to be marked by hand (slide and handout);
# with `counts` (id, label, n) each box shows how often the LLM chose that label.
coding_grid <- function(df, counts = NULL) {
  header <- paste0(
    '<th class="grid-tweet"></th>',
    paste0('<th class="grid-label"><div><span>', labels, "</span></div></th>", collapse = "")
  )
  cards <- tweet_html(df, numbered = TRUE)
  rows <- map2_chr(cards, df$id, \(card, id) {
    cells <- map_chr(labels, \(lab) {
      if (is.null(counts)) return('<td class="grid-cell"><span class="grid-box"></span></td>')
      n <- sum(counts$n[counts$id == id & counts$label == lab])
      paste0(
        '<td class="grid-cell"><span class="grid-box', if (n == 0) " zero" else if (n >= 3) " dark" else "",
        '" style="--share:', n / 5, '">', n, "</span></td>"
      )
    })
    paste0('<tr><td class="grid-tweet">', card, "</td>", paste(cells, collapse = ""), "</tr>")
  })
  paste0('<div class="coding-grid-wrap"><table class="coding-grid"><thead><tr>', header,
         "</tr></thead><tbody>", paste(rows, collapse = ""), "</tbody></table></div>")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: llm-setup
labels <- c("NATIONAL", "STATE", "LOCAL", "NON-POLITICAL", "UNCLEAR")

modal <- function(x) names(which.max(table(x)))

kripp_alpha <- function(id, label) {
  n_uc <- table(id, label) # tweets x labels: how many runs chose each label
  m <- rowSums(n_uc)
  n_uc <- n_uc[m > 1, , drop = FALSE]
  m <- m[m > 1]
  n <- sum(n_uc)
  observed <- sum(n_uc * (n_uc - 1) / (m - 1)) / n
  expected <- sum(colSums(n_uc) * (colSums(n_uc) - 1)) / (n * (n - 1))
  1 - (1 - observed) / (1 - expected)
}

per_tweet <- function(coded) {
  coded |>
    filter(!is.na(label)) |>
    summarise(
      n_labels = n_distinct(label),
      agreement = max(table(label)) / n(),
      labels = paste0(names(table(label)), " (", table(label), ")", collapse = ", "),
      .by = c(config, id)
    )
}

reliability <- function(coded) {
  coded <- filter(coded, !is.na(label))
  per_tweet(coded) |>
    summarise(identical = mean(n_labels == 1), .by = config) |>
    left_join(
      summarise(coded, alpha = kripp_alpha(id, label), .by = config),
      by = "config"
    )
}

plot_reliability <- function(summary, current) {
  summary |>
    mutate(
      config = factor(config, levels = rev(config)),
      current = config == .env$current,
      text = paste0(scales::percent(identical, accuracy = 1), "  (α = ", sprintf("%.2f", alpha), ")")
    ) |>
    ggplot(aes(identical, config)) +
    geom_col(aes(fill = current), width = 0.6) +
    geom_text(aes(label = text), hjust = -0.05, size = 6, color = "#333333") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = berkeley_blue, `FALSE` = muted), guide = "none") +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1.3), breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25)) +
    labs(x = "Tweets with the same label in all 5 runs", y = NULL)
}

# The model's probability of each label for one tweet (see label_probs() in llm_cache.R)
plot_probs <- function(probs, text = scales::percent(probs$p, accuracy = 1)) {
  probs |>
    mutate(label = factor(label, levels = rev(labels)), text = text) |>
    mutate(top = p == max(p), .by = any_of("prompt")) |>
    ggplot(aes(p, label)) +
    geom_col(aes(fill = top), width = 0.6) +
    geom_text(aes(label = text), hjust = -0.1, size = 6, color = "#333333") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = berkeley_blue, `FALSE` = muted), guide = "none") +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1.45), breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25)) +
    labs(x = "Probability of the label (one call)", y = NULL)
}

# Token probabilities come from Parasail: DeepInfra, which does the runs, doesn't return them.
# Same model, prompt, and settings as the runs; only the provider differs.
on_parasail <- function(chat) {
  chat_openrouter(
    system_prompt = chat$get_system_prompt(),
    model = chat$get_model(),
    params = params(temperature = 1),
    api_args = list(provider = list(
      order = list("Parasail"), allow_fallbacks = FALSE, require_parameters = TRUE
    ))
  )
}

# NATIONAL is tokenized as N + ATIONAL; NON-POLITICAL starts with its own token, NON
first_tokens <- c(NATIONAL = "N")

# Example tweet for the probability charts: a held-out tweet that falls under one of the new rules
example_id <- "1058137896912334848" # early voting for the legislator's own campaign: LOCAL under Rule 1
example <- filter(test, id_str == example_id)
```

[A common problem in social science research: **classifying documents by their content**.]{.pipe-footer}

## Lesson Overview

**Lesson:** Using LLMs to label and classify text

- LLMs good at "understanding" language
- fast and (relatively) cheap
- scales the codebook approach

**Goal:** labels you can **trust** and **defend** in a paper

## Components of the Lesson

1. **First API call:** prompt, system prompt, model settings, structured output
2. **Reliability:** the same label every time? ← *today*
3. **Validity:** do the labels match ground truth 
4. **Scaling up:** cost, caching, data privacy

. . .

## Learning Objectives

By the end of the lesson, you will be able to:

1. **label** text with an LLM through an API, choosing the prompt and settings
2. **assess** and **improve** the **reliability** of LLM labels ← *today*
3. **assess** the **validity** of LLM labels against ground truth 
4. **plan** a full labeling run: cost, data privacy, provider choice 

## Teaching Approach

- **real** dataset and research question
- **Exercise:** learn by **participating**
- build up **step by step**
- concepts introduced **when needed** 
- code shown for **conceptual understanding**

# Today's Component: How to make LLM measurement reliable

## Reliability and Validity

Common English words with **specific meanings** in social science research design:

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- **Reliability:** does the measurement give the *same result* every time?
- **Validity:** does it measure *what we want it to measure*?
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
#| label: reliability-validity
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6.6
#| fig-alt: "Four targets in a two-by-two grid. Not reliable and not valid: a wide scatter off to one side of the green bullseye. Reliable but not valid: a tight cluster away from the bullseye. Valid but not reliable: a wide scatter centered on the bullseye. Reliable and valid: a tight cluster on the bullseye."
#| out-width: 100%
library(ggplot2)

# Target radii ------------------------------------------------------------
r_inner  <- 1      # green bullseye
r_middle <- 2.4
r_outer  <- 4

# Colors ------------------------------------------------------------------
col_bullseye <- "#BFE08A"
col_valid    <- "#7AB82E"
col_reliable <- "#E8702A"
col_rings    <- "grey35"

# Panel centers -----------------------------------------------------------
x_left <- 0;  x_right <- 10.6
y_top  <- 10.4; y_bottom <- 0

# Helpers -----------------------------------------------------------------
circle <- function(r, n = 200) {
  t <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = n)
  data.frame(x = r * cos(t), y = r * sin(t))
}

# Evenly spread but irregular points in a disk (a jittered sunflower pattern),
# so a cloud really is centered where we say it is. Set `miss_bullseye = TRUE`
# to replace any shots that would land on the bullseye.
shots <- function(n, radius, center = c(0, 0), miss_bullseye = FALSE) {
  n_try <- if (miss_bullseye) 2 * n else n
  i <- seq_len(n_try)
  r <- radius * sqrt((i - 0.5) / n_try) * runif(n_try, 0.95, 1.03)
  a <- i * pi * (3 - sqrt(5)) + runif(n_try, -0.2, 0.2)
  d <- data.frame(x = r * cos(a) + center[1], y = r * sin(a) + center[2])
  if (miss_bullseye) {
    d <- d[sqrt(d$x^2 + d$y^2) > r_inner + 0.12, ]
    d <- d[sample(nrow(d), n), ]
  }
  d
}

place <- function(d, x0, y0) transform(d, x = x + x0, y = y + y0)

# Shots -------------------------------------------------------------------
set.seed(2026)
n_shots <- 20

# Wide scatter = about the size of the middle circle.
# Tight cluster = about the size of the bullseye.
points <- rbind(
  place(shots(n_shots, r_middle, c(-1.3, 1.3), miss_bullseye = TRUE), x_left, y_top),
  place(shots(n_shots, r_inner,  c(2.9, 0.8)),                            x_right, y_top),
  place(shots(n_shots, r_middle),                                       x_left, y_bottom),
  place(shots(n_shots, r_inner),                                        x_right, y_bottom)
)

# Targets -----------------------------------------------------------------
centers <- expand.grid(x0 = c(x_left, x_right), y0 = c(y_top, y_bottom))

bullseyes <- do.call(rbind, Map(function(x0, y0, id) {
  transform(place(circle(r_inner), x0, y0), id = id)
}, centers$x0, centers$y0, seq_len(nrow(centers))))

rings <- do.call(rbind, Map(function(x0, y0, id) {
  rbind(
    transform(place(circle(r_inner),  x0, y0), id = paste(id, "inner")),
    transform(place(circle(r_middle), x0, y0), id = paste(id, "middle")),
    transform(place(circle(r_outer),  x0, y0), id = paste(id, "outer"))
  )
}, centers$x0, centers$y0, seq_len(nrow(centers))))

# Plot --------------------------------------------------------------------
pad <- 0.6

ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = bullseyes, aes(x, y, group = id), fill = col_bullseye) +
  geom_path(data = rings, aes(x, y, group = id), color = col_rings, linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(data = points, aes(x, y), size = 1.7, color = "black") +
  # Overlapping rectangles: right column = reliable, bottom row = valid
  annotate("rect",
    xmin = x_right - r_outer - pad, xmax = x_right + r_outer + pad,
    ymin = y_bottom - r_outer - pad, ymax = y_top + r_outer + 2.4,
    fill = NA, color = col_reliable, linewidth = 1.3) +
  annotate("rect",
    xmin = x_left - r_outer - 4.6, xmax = x_right + r_outer + pad + 0.3,
    ymin = y_bottom - r_outer - pad - 0.3, ymax = y_bottom + r_outer + pad,
    fill = NA, color = col_valid, linewidth = 1.3) +
  # Labels
  annotate("text", x = c(x_left, x_right), y = y_top + r_outer + 1.3,
    label = c("Not Reliable", "Reliable"),
    size = 7, fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("text", x = x_left - r_outer - 0.6, y = c(y_top, y_bottom),
    label = c("Not Valid", "Valid"),
    size = 7, fontface = "bold", hjust = 1) +
  coord_fixed(clip = "off") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    plot.background  = element_rect(fill = "transparent", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", color = NA)
  )
```
:::

We force the model to answer with exactly one of these (**structured output**).

## Reliability

Remember that an LLM is **probabilistic**: it picks the next "token" by sampling from a probability distribution.

```{r}
#| label: chat-simple-early
#| ref.label: chat-simple
#| echo: false
```

```{r}

example_probs <- list(
  "Simple prompt" = cached_probs(on_parasail(chat_simple), type, example, first_tokens)
) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "prompt")
```

```{r}

```

```{r}

#| fig-height: 2.6
plot_probs(filter(example_probs, prompt == "Simple prompt"))
```

## Reliability

So each time we run, **even with the same settings**, the same tweet might be classified differently.

Here we'll see how we can **increase the reliability** of the labeling.

. . .

::: callout-box
Reliable is not the same as **valid**. A model can give the same answer every time and still be wrong. Validity is the next component.
:::

## Step 1: Simple Prompt

```{r}
#| label: chat-simple
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "|1-2|4-6|8-17|9|10"
simple_prompt <- "Classify this tweet from a U.S. state legislator as
NATIONAL, STATE, LOCAL, NON-POLITICAL, or UNCLEAR."

type <- type_object(
  label = type_enum(c("NATIONAL", "STATE", "LOCAL", "NON-POLITICAL", "UNCLEAR"))
)

chat_simple <- chat_openrouter(
  system_prompt = simple_prompt,
  model = "qwen/qwen3-235b-a22b-2507",
  params = params(temperature = 1),
  api_args = list(provider = list(
    order = list("DeepInfra"), allow_fallbacks = FALSE, require_parameters = TRUE
  ))
)
```

```{r}
#| label: dev-results
# Label each dev tweet 5 times with chat_simple; each tweet-run pair is only sent to the API once (see llm_cache.R)
simple_dev <- cached_labels(chat_simple, type, dev)

dev_results <- simple_dev |>
  mutate(config = "1. Simple prompt", label = as.character(label))
```

## Step 2: Specific Prompt

How do we come up with a more specific prompt?

- Look at the tweets that were **labeled differently across runs**: that's where the model is uncertain
- Encode what we learn into the prompt: **definitions** and **rules for borderline cases**

. . .

This is how **codebooks** are created to make inter-coder reliability high.

```{r}
#| label: themes
flippers <- dev_tweets |>
  filter(n_labels > 1) |>
  left_join(select(dev, id = id_str, everything()), by = "id")

# Themes identified by reading the tweets that got different labels across runs
themes <- list(
  district = c("1051126532532592640", "975324133864214528"),
  levels   = c("689938129269190656", "796146585805656064"),
  politics = c("1096137071406862336", "1091799424873971712"),
  unclear  = c("1237381936072531968")
)
stopifnot(all(unlist(themes) %in% flippers$id)) # fails if the cached simple-prompt runs change

theme_tweets <- function(theme) {
  flippers |>
    filter(id %in% themes[[theme]]) |>
    arrange(match(id, themes[[theme]]))
}

# The model's probabilities for the theme tweets, on one call with the simple prompt
theme_probs <- cached_probs(
  on_parasail(chat_simple), type, filter(dev, id_str %in% unlist(themes)), first_tokens
)

theme_cards <- function(theme) {
  theme_tweets(theme) |>
    # Shorten a long quoted tweet so the slide fits without scrolling
    mutate(quoted_status.full_text = if_else(
      id == "975324133864214528",
      sub("\\(GA House -Dist 49\\).*$", "(GA House -Dist 49) ...", quoted_status.full_text),
      quoted_status.full_text
    )) |>
    rename(id_str = id) |>
    tweet_cards(show_labels = TRUE, probs = theme_probs)
}
```

## Where Did the Model Disagree With Itself?

`r nrow(flippers)` of `r n_per_set` tweets got different labels across the 5 runs.

<br>

Reading them, some **themes** emerge

## Theme 1: My District or My State? {.scrollable}

Legislators talk about **their own district and their own seat** in the state legislature. Is that LOCAL or STATE?

```{r}
#| label: theme-district
#| output: asis
theme_cards("district")
```

## Theme 2: Whose Decision Is It? {.scrollable}

A **place** at one level and an **actor** at another: a state agency in one district, a presidential vote in one precinct.

```{r}
#| label: theme-levels
#| output: asis
theme_cards("levels")
```

## Theme 3: Is This Political? {.scrollable}

Holidays and scenery that **mention** something political but make **no political point**.

```{r}
#| label: theme-politics
#| output: asis
theme_cards("politics")
```

## Theme 4: Nothing to Go On {.scrollable}

The meaning depends on **something the model can't see**: a photo, a link, an earlier tweet in a thread.

```{r}
#| label: theme-unclear
#| output: asis
theme_cards("unclear")
```

## Step 2: A Rule for Each Theme

```{r}
#| label: specific-prompt
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "|1-2|5-6|7-9|10-11|12-13"
specific_prompt <- "Classify this tweet from a U.S. state legislator as
NATIONAL, STATE, LOCAL, NON-POLITICAL, or UNCLEAR.

Rules for borderline cases:
1. The legislator's own district, constituents, or campaign for their seat is LOCAL,
   even when the tweet mentions their seat in the state legislature.
2. When a tweet mixes levels, choose the level of the main actor or decision, not
   the place: a state agency working in one county is STATE; a presidential
   election result in one precinct is NATIONAL.
3. Holidays, commemorations, greetings, jokes, and scenery are NON-POLITICAL
   unless the tweet makes a policy or political point.
4. If the meaning depends on something you cannot see (a photo, a link, or an
   earlier tweet in a thread), choose UNCLEAR."
```

## Step 2: Same Code, New Prompt

```{r}
#| label: chat-specific
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "2"
chat_specific <- chat_openrouter(
  system_prompt = specific_prompt,
  model = "qwen/qwen3-235b-a22b-2507",
  params = params(temperature = 1),
  api_args = list(provider = list(
    order = list("DeepInfra"), allow_fallbacks = FALSE, require_parameters = TRUE
  ))
)
```

```{r}
#| label: run-test-step2
# The test tweets, labeled 5 times with each prompt (cached, like the development tweets)
test_results <- list(
  "1. Simple prompt"   = cached_labels(chat_simple, type, test),
  "2. Specific prompt" = cached_labels(chat_specific, type, test)
) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "config")
```

## Step 2 Results: `r n_per_set` New Tweets

Compared on **held-out tweets**, so the specific prompt wasn't written with these tweets in mind.

```{r}
#| label: results-step2
plot_reliability(reliability(test_results), current = "2. Specific prompt")
```

  facet_wrap(~prompt) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1.6), breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1))

## Step 3: top-k = 1

With **top-k = 1**, the model can only pick the **single most likely** next token.

Our example tweet with the **simple prompt**:

```{r}
#| label: topk-plot
#| fig-height: 2.6
simple_example <- filter(example_probs, prompt == "Simple prompt")
plot_probs(
  simple_example,
  text = if_else(simple_example$p == max(simple_example$p), "always chosen", "never chosen")
)
```

## Step 3: Same Code, One New Setting

```{r}
#| label: chat-topk
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "4"
chat_topk <- chat_openrouter(
  system_prompt = specific_prompt,
  model = "qwen/qwen3-235b-a22b-2507",
  params = params(temperature = 1, top_k = 1),
  api_args = list(provider = list(
    order = list("DeepInfra"), allow_fallbacks = FALSE, require_parameters = TRUE
  ))
)
```

```{r}
#| label: run-test-step3
test_results <- bind_rows(
  test_results,
  cached_labels(chat_topk, type, test) |> mutate(config = "3. + top-k = 1")
)
```

## Step 3 Results

```{r}
#| label: results-step3
plot_reliability(reliability(test_results), current = "3. + top-k = 1")
```

## Why Is It Still Not 100%?

```{r}
#| label: still-flipping
still_flipping <- per_tweet(filter(test_results, config == "3. + top-k = 1")) |>
  filter(n_labels > 1)
```

`r nrow(still_flipping)` of `r n_per_set` tweets still get different labels across runs, even though the model always picks the most likely token:

- **Near-ties:** when two labels are almost equally likely, tiny numerical differences decide
- **Hardware is not deterministic:** GPUs batch requests together, and floating-point math gives slightly different probabilities from run to run
- **Providers change:** model versions, hardware, and quantization can change without notice

## Further Steps

- **continue improving prompt**
- **few-shot prompting:** give the model labeled borderline cases
- **majority vote:** run each tweet several times and take the most common label
- **better model:** some LLMs are better at understanding context and following prompts

## {visibility="uncounted"}

```{r}
#| label: by-state-data
# Side analysis of the second research question; the labels come from state_national/analysis.R
by_state_tweets <- readr::read_csv("state_national/results/labels.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(national = as.integer(label == "NATIONAL"), log10_pop = log10(population))
by_state <- readr::read_csv("state_national/results/by_state.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Linear probability models with standard errors clustered by state, since population only varies between states
clustered <- function(model) {
  lmtest::coeftest(model, vcov = sandwich::vcovCL(model, cluster = ~legislator_state))
}
state_models <- list(
  "All tweets" = lm(national ~ log10_pop, data = by_state_tweets),
  "Political tweets" = lm(national ~ log10_pop, data = filter(by_state_tweets, label %in% c("NATIONAL", "STATE", "LOCAL")))
)
slope <- clustered(state_models[["All tweets"]])["log10_pop", "Estimate"]
fitted_range <- range(fitted(state_models[["All tweets"]]))
```

## Appendix: Do Smaller States Talk About National Matters More? {visibility="uncounted"}

- **Sample:** 200 random tweets per state, `r scales::comma(nrow(by_state_tweets))` in all
- **Labels:** our final configuration (specific prompt + top-k = 1), one run
- **Population:** Census Bureau estimates, July 1, 2020
- **Model:** NATIONAL or not, on log~10~ population

**Result:** a state 10 times larger has **`r round(-100 * slope, 1)` points fewer** NATIONAL tweets (`r scales::percent(fitted_range[2], accuracy = 1)` in Wyoming, `r scales::percent(fitted_range[1], accuracy = 1)` in California).

## Appendix: Regression Results {visibility="uncounted"}

Linear probability model: is the tweet labeled NATIONAL?

::: {style="font-size: 0.75em"}
```{r}
#| label: by-state-table
format_coef <- function(model, term) {
  ct <- clustered(model)
  stars <- cut(ct[term, 4], c(-Inf, 0.001, 0.01, 0.05, Inf), c("***", "**", "*", ""))
  paste0(sprintf("%.3f", ct[term, 1]), stars, "<br>(", sprintf("%.3f", ct[term, 2]), ")")
}
tibble(
  ` ` = c("log<sub>10</sub>(population)", "Intercept", "Tweets", "States"),
  !!!map(state_models, \(m) c(
    format_coef(m, "log10_pop"), format_coef(m, "(Intercept)"),
    scales::comma(nobs(m)), "50"
  ))
) |>
  knitr::kable(format = "html", escape = FALSE, align = c("l", "c", "c"))
```

Standard errors clustered by state in parentheses. \*p < 0.05, \*\*p < 0.01, \*\*\*p < 0.001. Political tweets: those labeled NATIONAL, STATE, or LOCAL.
:::
